title: Ultra-Processed
subtitle: A word used everywhere. Defined almost nowhere.
description: BOTIA uses this term across the whole site. This page explains what it actually means — and what BOTIA can and cannot say about it.
what_body: Ultra-processed is not a judgement or a marketing word. It comes from NOVA, a classification developed at the University of São Paulo and adopted by FAO and WHO in their 2019 report. NOVA does not classify food by nutrients — by calories, fat or sugar. It classifies by how much industrial processing a food has undergone, and by whether it contains substances never used in home cooking.
group1_desc: Fruit, vegetables, eggs, milk, meat, grains. Cleaned, cut, frozen or pasteurised, but nothing added.
group2_desc: Oil, butter, sugar, salt. Extracted from Group 1 foods and used to cook, not eaten alone.
group3_desc: Bread, cheese, tinned vegetables, cured meat. Group 1 plus Group 2, with few ingredients and recognisable origins.
group4_desc: Industrial formulations containing substances you would never find in a kitchen: flavourings, emulsifiers, thickeners, colourings, sweeteners and protein isolates.
highlight_text: The difference between Group 3 and Group 4 is not how healthy something is. It is whether the ingredient list contains substances that exist only because industry needs them — to bind, to preserve, to colour, or to make something taste like what it no longer is.
markers_body: The three evidence layers BOTIA uses are, in fact, the three groups of substances NOVA names as characteristic of ultra-processing. This is not a coincidence — it is the same criterion approached from the label.
why_body: The relevance of NOVA is that it looks at the whole, not the parts. A product can be low in sugar, low in fat, high in protein — and still be a Group 4 formulation. Nutritional labelling was not designed to show that. The ingredient list was never meant to be read as a whole either. BOTIA reads it as a whole.
can_1: Detect individual ingredients that NOVA describes as markers of ultra-processing.
can_2: Show how many of those markers appear on a single label.
can_3: Explain what each one is doing there and where it comes from.
cannot_1: Assign a NOVA group to a product — BOTIA reads ingredients, not whole formulations.
cannot_2: Know the industrial processes used, which the label never declares.
cannot_3: Tell you whether a product is good or bad for you. That is not a classification question.
closing: BOTIA does not classify products. It reads what the label declares and tells you what it means. The conclusion is yours.
